# Common-cap targets, exact saturation retargeting, and the remaining deficit

This note gives exact sufficient favorable-menu criteria in the positive-width model. It does not infer a movable active family from a Hessian kernel. All menus consist of actual minimizing through-source caps.

## 1. One common INTERIOR target point is enough

Fix an actual source \(Y=(p,y)\), and a balanced finite active menu with response weights \(\nu_j>0\), \(\sum\nu_j=1\). Let \(q\) be an exposed vertex of the COMPLETE sampled-base hull. Suppose there is \(x_*\in\operatorname{int}K_q\) such that every menu cap has nonnegative physical margin at \((q,x_*)\):
\[
a_j\cdot(q-p)+u_j\cdot(x_*-y)+b\geq0. \tag{1}
\]
Here \(\Gamma(u_j)=1\); \(b=0\) in the pure-width problem, and \(b=\epsilon f_H(Y)\geq0\) in the buffered one.

Choose the ordinary projective-energy normalizer \(P_*(x)>0\) on \(K_q\), centered at \(x_*\), so that the projective image has centroid zero. Its normal-dependent cone field is
\[
F_q(n,x)=[h_{K_q}(n)-n\cdot x_*]P_*(x)^{-d}.
\]
The finite convex extension and exposed-base gap construction give an admissible nonnegative physical field \(\Phi_q\), supported exactly on the measured \(q\)-fiber normal bundle and agreeing there with \(F_q\).

By (1), each smooth cap dominates the indicator of its through-\(x_*\) halfspace on \(K_q\). Projective cone integration and ordinary centroid Grünbaum give
\[
\int\Phi_q\Psi_j\,d\sigma\geq\Gamma_d\int\Phi_q\,d\sigma
\]
for EVERY menu term. Their response-weighted average has the same exact efficiency. This criterion is strictly weaker than requiring an entire target fiber to be captured.

If each source has such a target, sum one normalized field per SOURCE. The sum uses at most \(k(P)\) fields and gives the simultaneous \(\Gamma_d/k(P)\) capture credit, subject only to the already explicit small width/buffer response corrections. Two sources may use the same target fiber but different common points and projective normalizers, so their two fields cannot in general be identified. A reduction to one field per distinct target is justified only when that same field is proved to pay each source using it, as in the common-symmetry theorem.

## 2. Affine form of a minimal continuous circuit

Assume a quantile menu has \(r+1\) continuous normals spanning rank \(r\), with its unique positive dependence
\[
\sum_j\rho_j u_j=0,\qquad \rho_j>0,\quad \sum_j\rho_j=1.
\]
In the pure-width model its margins are
\[
m_j(z,x)=a_j\cdot(z-p)+u_j\cdot(x-y).
\]
Set
\[
s(z)=\sum_j\rho_j a_j\cdot(z-p).
\]
The vector \((s(z)-a_j\cdot(z-p))_j\) is orthogonal to \(\rho\), and the map \(v\mapsto(u_j\cdot v)_j\) has precisely that range. Choose a linear right inverse on this range and define an affine map \(c(z)\), with \(c(p)=y\), satisfying
\[
u_j\cdot(c(z)-y)=s(z)-a_j\cdot(z-p).
\]
Then
\[
m_j(z,x)=u_j\cdot(x-c(z))+s(z). \tag{2}
\]
The map \(c\) is determined modulo the common continuous kernel. Thus \(s(z)\geq0\) and \(c(z)\in\operatorname{int}K_z\) suffice for the common-cap criterion. More generally the simplex/cylinder \(\{m_j\geq0\ \forall j\}\) may meet \(\operatorname{int}K_z\) away from \(c(z)\).

Formula (2) is purely linear algebra. It does NOT prove that the affine circuit center lies in any target fiber. The common-symmetry theorem supplies exactly this missing inclusion in its stated symmetric class.

## 3. The pure-base saturation baseline

Let all sampled fibers have positive volumes \(V_z\), and fix a source base \(p\). Consider generic base vectors \(a\), meaning \(a\cdot(z-p)\ne0\) for every \(z\ne p\). There are finitely many sign cells. Define
\[
B_p=\min_{a\ {\rm generic}}\ \sum_{\{z:\ a\cdot(z-p)>0\}}V_z. \tag{3}
\]
For a singleton base set put \(B_p=0\).

Fix a vector \(a_*\) attaining (3). For ANY fixed normalized continuous direction \(u\), a sufficiently large finite multiple \(t a_*\) makes the smooth integrand identically one on every positive-sign fiber and zero on every negative-sign fiber. Compactness and finite nonzero base gaps prove this simultaneously across each entire fiber. The own-fiber cap is unchanged.

Write \(Q_p^{\rm own}(u)\) for the actual own-fiber smoothed mass at the fixed source mark and \(Q\) for its mixed depth. It follows for every \(u\) that
\[
Q\leq Q_p^{\rm own}(u)+B_p. \tag{4}
\]
If \(N=(a,u)\) is ACTUALLY active, let \(Q_p^{\rm out}(N)\) be its mass outside the source fiber. Since \(Q=Q_p^{\rm own}(u)+Q_p^{\rm out}(N)\), (4) yields
\[
0\leq Q_p^{\rm out}(N)\leq B_p,
\qquad
\Delta_N:=B_p-Q_p^{\rm out}(N)
       =B_p+Q_p^{\rm own}(u)-Q\geq0. \tag{5}
\]
No saturation of the original active cap is needed for this inequality.

Whenever \(\Delta_N=0\), replace its base tilt by the finite saturating multiple of the SAME vector \(a_*\). The cap mass remains exactly \(Q\), so the replacement is active. It retains its normalized continuous direction. Hence any balanced quantile menu supported on \(\{\Delta_N=0\}\) can be retargeted this way and remains balanced. Its new response weights are obtained from its new positive coareas by the exact coarea conversion; they need not equal the old response weights.

If \(B_p>0\), choose a vertex \(q\) maximizing \(a_*\cdot z\). The maximum relative to \(p\) is positive, and the retargeted caps all capture the ENTIRE \(q\)-fiber. Their menu has efficiency one under any nonzero nonnegative field isolating that exposed fiber.

If \(B_p=0\), all other fibers lie strictly on the negative side for a minimizing generic vector, so \(p\) is itself an exposed complete-base vertex. The own-source projective transfer then gives efficiency \(\Gamma_d\) for every active menu.

Thus a balanced menu supported on zero saturation deficit is a rigorous paying case.

## 4. A precise unresolved alternative

The active representative set is compact and (5) is continuous in its normalized continuous direction. In the pure-width model let \(\mathcal R_p\) be the compact set of balanced quantile probability menus, \(\int u\,d\rho=0\). Define
\[
D_p=\min_{\rho\in\mathcal R_p}\int\Delta_N\,d\rho(N).
\]
The minimum exists. Since \(\Delta_N\geq0\), \(D_p=0\) holds exactly when there is a balanced menu supported on the zero-deficit active caps. Section 3 pays that case. If no such menu exists, then \(D_p>0\).

This last positive deficit is an exact numerical invariant of the full active-cap family. It is not automatically a lower bound on proper outside section mass. A positive deficit may come from a fully saturated pattern which is realized using the continuous coordinates but is cheaper than every generic pure-base pattern. Nor does a positive or zero normal Hessian identify its value.

A complete next step would have to pay this positive-deficit alternative using actual convex geometry or body variation. No such payment is asserted here. In particular the note does not turn a local flat saturation cell into a global retargeting theorem.
